name: Nepali
family: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan (Northern zone, Eastern Pahari)
variety: Standard Nepali, the eastern dialect used by educated speakers and in the national media (Khatiwada 2009)
sources: Khatiwada, Rajesh (2009). Nepali. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(3), 373-380.
Pokharel, Madhav Prasad (1989). Experimental Analysis of Nepali Sound System. PhD dissertation, University of Pune.
Bandhu, Chudamani; Dahal, Ballabh Mani; Holzhausen, Andreas & Hale, Austin (1971). Nepali Segmental Phonology. Kirtipur: Summer Institute of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University.

Clements, George N. & Khatiwada, Rajesh (2007). Phonetic realization of contrastively aspirated affricates in Nepali. Proceedings of the 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Saarbrücken, 629-632.
Acharya, Jayaraj (1991). A Descriptive Grammar of Nepali and an Analyzed Corpus. Washington: Georgetown University Press.
Riccardi, Theodore (2003). Nepali. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2016). The intonation of South Asian languages: towards a comparative analysis. Proceedings of Formal Approaches to South Asian Languages 6, 23-36.
contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced (/tsar/ 'four', /tsʰar/ 'ash', /dzar/ 'lover', /dzʱar/ 'weed')
dental versus retroflex stops; the retroflexes are only weakly retroflex (apical postalveolar)
affricates are laminal alveolar /ts tsʰ dz dzʱ/, not palatal
six oral vowels; five of them have nasal counterparts (there is no /õ/)
no vowel length contrast, although the script writes long and short i and u
only two fricatives /s ɦ/: the letters श ष स are all [s] in ordinary speech
allophony: /ɖ/ is a retroflex flap [ɽ] after a vowel (/ɡʱoɖa/ [ɡʱoɽa] 'horse', /tsʰoɖnu/ [tsʰoɽnu] 'to leave'); it stays a stop initially and when geminate
breathy voiced stops often lose their aspiration between vowels and word-finally and are made with a looser closure (/bagʱ/ [baɡʱ] or [baɡ] 'tiger')
aspirated labials and velars may be fricatives in running speech: /pʰ/ [ɸ], /bʱ/ [β], /kʰ/ [x], /ɡʱ/ [ɣ]
/r/ is a short trill word-initially, a single tap between vowels and finally, a strong trill when geminate
/ɦ/ is voiced or voiceless depending on the speaker; between vowels it may drop with lengthening of the vowel (/pʌɦaɖi/ [paːɽi])
vowels after aspirated stops, voiced or voiceless, begin with breathy voice and lowered F0 (Clements & Khatiwada 2007)
/ʌ/ is slightly rounded in isolation, lower and further back than a schwa, and varies widely with context
[j w] are non-syllabic variants of /i u/ next to vowels
a retroflex nasal flap occurs only before retroflex stops and in spelling pronunciations of Sanskrit loans
any vowel is slightly nasalised next to a nasal consonant
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C); initial clusters only with /r/ or a glide as second member, and many speakers break stop plus /r/ with a vowel ([prʌdʱan] or [pʌrdʱan])
phonotactics: /ŋ/ occurs only word-finally, apart from a few onomatopoeic words
geminates occur only medially and do not undergo lenition
the inherent vowel /ʌ/ is dropped at the end of most nouns but kept in many verb forms and after clusters (छ [tsʰʌ], गर्छ [ɡʌrtsʰʌ]); the script does not show which

stress.rule: Stress and pitch are non-distinctive (Khatiwada 2009); descriptions place a weak prominence on the first syllable, where the low target of the phrasal rise is aligned.
stress.cues: not established instrumentally; pitch (low start of the rising phrase)

rhythm.notes: Class and final lengthening are assumptions from the areal pattern; no measurement could be verified.

length.notes: No vowel length contrast; a few long vowels arise from loss of intervocalic /ɦ/. All consonants except /ɦ/ and the glides have geminate counterparts; no duration figures could be verified.

intonation.declarative: a chain of rising phrases, one per content word with its clitics, low on the first syllable and high on the last; the final phrase falls to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: rising phrases and a high final boundary
intonation.wh_question: as a declarative, low final boundary
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases; low-rising boundary at clause ends
intonation.accent_shape: L* ... H per phrase, with the peak at the end of the phrase; as an alternative the peak comes early, on the second or third syllable (L*+H)
intonation.notes: Rising phrases and the two peak alignments are from Khan 2016 (recording of Khatiwada 2009); the sentence-type boundary tones are the typical South Asian pattern given there, not a separate Nepali study.

phonation: breathy voiced stops and affricates /bʱ d̪ʱ dzʱ ɖʱ ɡʱ/, produced with a larger glottal opening than the plain voiced series
breathy voice on the first part of vowels after both voiced and voiceless aspirates

problems: The affricates are the Hindi palatals (च [c], छ [cʰ], ज [ɟ], झ [ɟʰ]); Nepali has laminal alveolar [ts tsʰ dz dzʱ].
श and ष are [ʃ] and [ʂ] (देश [deːʃ], विषय [wɪʂəjə]); Nepali speakers have [s].

Long Hindi vowels eː, oː, aː are used beside short i, u although Nepali has no length contrast; औ is the monophthong [ɔː] and final ौं is [ɔːn] (काठमाडौं [kaːʈʰəmaːɖɔːn]) instead of a diphthong [ʌu] and a nasal vowel.
Word-final र keeps the inherent vowel: घर is [ɡʰʌɾə].
The infinitive ending -नु comes out with two vowels: गर्नु [ɡʌrrnuʲu].
Allophony is missing: /ɖ/ after a vowel stays a stop (पढ्नु [pʌɖʰnu...]), breathy stops are not weakened between vowels, aspirates are not spirantised.
Breathy voiced stops come from the Hindi base table (voiced closure plus voiceless aspiration sample); no breathy vowel onset.
Intonation uses the generic eSpeak tunes; no rising phrase on each content word.
good: the inherent vowel is a backed schwa, close to Nepali /ʌ/
the phoneme table defines the Nepali diphthongs (ʌi, ʌu, ei, eu, oi, ou, ui)
equal length settings for stressed and unstressed syllables suit the weak stress

notes: Khatiwada's speaker regularly used voiceless [h] for /ɦ/. Pokharel 1989 counts ten diphthongs; many vowel sequences can also be analysed as two syllables. The vowel chart in Khatiwada 2009 is based on five male speakers but gives no formant table, so vowel_formants is left out, as is VOT.
